name: Backcombing

card.summary: A hairstyling technique that combs strands toward the scalp to tangle and lift them, adding volume and height at the crown.
card.note: Repeated backcombing is reported to rub the hair cuticle and cause breakage.

quick.overview:
Backcombing, also called teasing or ratting, is a way to add volume by combing hair repeatedly toward the roots. The tangled base holds the hair up, creating lift at the crown or fullness through the lengths.

It is behind big-hair looks such as beehives and bouffants and is used by musicians and stylists. For looks it offers instant body for fine or flat hair. Dermatology literature mentions it among practices to avoid in fragile hair.
quick.how: A section of hair is held away from the head and combed back toward the scalp so that short tangles form at the base, then the surface is smoothed over the top. Stylists often follow it with hairspray to hold the shape.
quick.risks: The technique rubs against the hair cuticle, and repeated use is described as causing progressive damage, weakening and breakage. It can leave root tangles that are hard to remove, and dermatology reviews of fragile hair disorders list backcombing among practices to avoid.

lead: Backcombing is a hairstyling technique for adding volume. Hair is combed repeatedly toward the scalp, which tangles the strands near the root and lifts the hair above it. It is also known as teasing or ratting.[1]

People use it for height and body in styles such as the beehive and bouffant, and it is associated with entertainers including Amy Winehouse, Cyndi Lauper, The Ronettes and Robert Smith.[1] For someone with fine or flat hair it gives instant lift that holds a shape through the day, usually with hairspray. The same crown lift also changes the look of head and face proportions, which is why it features in both vintage and alternative styling.
The same rubbing action that creates volume is reported to wear on the hair's cuticle and, with repetition, to cause progressive damage and breakage.[1]

angle.text: Backcombing gives immediate volume and height without products or heat. It is used at the crown for lift or through the lengths for a big-hair look.

paras: The core action is repeated combing toward the roots, which tangles the strands and creates a cushion of lift. It is a general method rather than a fixed procedure, and stylists adapt it to the hair type and the style.[1]

In the classic method described for the bouffant, hair on top of the head is backcombed into a loosely knotted pile, and the smooth outer hair is then combed over it for a sleek finish, with the ends curled, flipped or cut as the style requires.[3] Wiglets or nylon mesh cushions can add height at the crown, and a rattail comb is used to lift hair back into place because brushing would flatten the style.[3]

The voluminous bouffant descends from the 18th-century pouf, worn by aristocrats on wigs and hairpieces, and returned in the Belle Epoque, the Gibson Girl era and the Edwardian period, when hair waxes, fixatives and hairpieces added volume.[3] British stylist Raymond Bessone is credited with reviving it in the 1950s, in a version nicknamed teasy-weasy.[3]

The bouffant peaked in the 1960s. Jacqueline Kennedy's low bouffant raised its profile in the United States, and girl groups such as the Supremes, the Ronettes, the Shirelles and Martha and the Vandellas wore it, with sales of rollers and hairspray rising significantly.[3] The taller beehive is credited to Margaret Vinci Heldt of Elmhurst, Illinois, who created it in 1960 after Modern Beauty Salon magazine asked her to design a style for the coming decade; a reporter's remark that it looked like a beehive gave it its name.[4] Backcombing is the construction step of the beehive, and Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961) and Brigitte Bardot are among those who popularised the look.[4]

Amy Winehouse revived the beehive in the 2000s, inspired by Ronnie Spector, and the 2010s retro and rockabilly trends brought bouffants and pompadours back.[3][4] Wikipedia also lists Siouxsie Sioux and Robert Smith among backcombing's alternative-music wearers, and notes its role in dreadlock formation.[1]

Backcombing is part of big-hair styles such as beehives, bouffants and dreadlocks.[1] It is used for crown lift, for fullness through the lengths, and as a base under which hair is smoothed. Hairspray holds the result; it was first packaged in the US in 1948 and by 1964 was reported to be the highest-selling beauty product, a rise that coincided with the teased styles of the era.[5] Hair spray polymers give hair structural support and protect shape against humidity and wind.[5]

Backcombing rubs against the hair cuticle, and the Wikipedia article states it can cause serious and progressive damage, weakening hair and causing breakage; frequent use is therefore described as unsuitable for people who want to keep long hair, and root tangles can be hard to remove.[1] A pediatric dermatology review of congenital hair shaft disorders lists backcombing, brushing, chemical products, tight braids and heat among practices to avoid for fragile hair.[2]

No studies found on backcombing itself. A review of hair shaft disorders with fragility recommends gentle hair care without backcombing, but it concerns congenital conditions and is based on case reports and small series.[2]

timeline.event: Chase Products is first to package hairspray in the US.[5]
Raymond Bessone is credited with reviving the bouffant for women.[3]
Margaret Vinci Heldt creates the beehive in Chicago.[4]
Audrey Hepburn wears a beehive in Breakfast at Tiffany's.[4]
Hairspray is reported as the highest-selling beauty product.[5]
